screens.title: Basic Physics, Collision Detection, and User Input
screens.subtitle: How Rigidbody, Colliders, and Input work together to make interactive game characters

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn the core building blocks that make movement and interactions feel real in Unity. We start with the Rigidbody component, the bridge between your object and Unity's physics engine, and see why adding forces and using the right lifecycle method leads to smooth, predictable motion. You'll learn how Colliders let objects detect contact or serve as trigger zones, and how to pick the right mode when you want physical impact versus event detection. The legacy Input Manager gives simple, smoothed axis values for natural movement, and combining those axis values with Rigidbody methods is a common, robust pattern. I'll show concrete code for a player controller, explain common mistakes like moving physics objects via transform, and give quick troubleshooting checks when collisions don't fire. By the end you will understand when to use AddForce versus setting velocity, how triggers differ from collisions, and how FixedUpdate keeps physics stable. Think about a player capsule that walks, jumps, and collects items — this chapter shows the exact components and code to make that happen reliably.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Rigidbody hands control to the physics engine; Colliders define shapes for collisions or triggers; use FixedUpdate and Input.GetAxis for stable character movement.

Physics stack
Rigidbody → Collider → Callbacks → Input
Attach a Rigidbody to let Unity move the object with gravity and forces. Add a Collider to detect contact. Use callbacks for events, and read Input axes to drive forces or velocity.
Quick tip
Never move physics objects by setting transform.position; use Rigidbody methods in FixedUpdate for stable collisions.
Common mistake
Forgetting a Rigidbody on either object prevents collision callbacks. If collisions don't fire, check for missing Rigidbodies or wrongly set Is Trigger flags.

narration.text: These objectives map to the practical skills you'll need to build a physics-driven player. First, you'll explain how Rigidbody works in both 2D and 3D and why attaching the correct Rigidbody type matters for your project. Second, you'll apply forces and manipulate velocity through Rigidbody methods, understanding the difference between AddForce and directly setting velocity. Third, you'll distinguish between collision callbacks and trigger callbacks and write simple handlers for each. Fourth, you'll configure Colliders so they detect interactions reliably without unwanted passthrough. Each objective includes a short practice step so you can verify competency. For example, attach a Rigidbody to a capsule and watch gravity apply. If the capsule doesn't move, check that the Rigidbody type matches the project (2D vs 3D) and that gravity is enabled. These skills let you create believable movement, reliable pickups, and predictable physical interactions that are essential for most games.

screens.title: What is a Rigidbody?
screens.subtitle: How Rigidbody connects your GameObject to Unity's physics engine

narration.text: A Rigidbody is the component that hands control of an object’s motion to Unity’s physics engine. When a Rigidbody is attached, the engine applies gravity, resolves collisions, and responds to forces, rather than you manually updating positions. For 2D projects use Rigidbody2D; for 3D use Rigidbody. A concrete example is a capsule player that falls naturally when gravity is enabled on its Rigidbody and collides with a ground collider without manual position changes. A common misconception is that adding a Collider alone makes an object dynamic; a Collider without a Rigidbody acts as a static obstacle and will not move in response to physics. Another pitfall is mixing direct transform changes with Rigidbody physics; doing so can produce jitter and missed collisions. Key properties you will use are mass, drag, and constraints — mass affects acceleration under force, drag resists motion, and constraints freeze unwanted axes. Try adding a Rigidbody to a scene object, toggle Use Gravity, and observe how it begins to fall and respond. This confirms the Rigidbody is the correct entry point for physical interactions. What is a Rigidbody? means rigidbody gives an object physical behavior — gravity, forces, and reactions — and requires using physics-aware methods rather than transform changes.. In practical terms, how rigidbody connects your gameobject to unity's physics engine. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Rigidbody gives an object physical behavior — gravity, forces, and reactions — and requires using physics-aware methods rather than transform changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a Rigidbody?
Rigidbody explained
Rigidbody hands motion control to Unity's physics. Use Rigidbody2D for 2D games and Rigidbody for 3D projects.
  • Mass affects how forces change velocity.
  • Drag resists motion; angular drag resists rotation.
  • Constraints freeze position or rotation axes to prevent unwanted motion.
Common mistakes
Moving physics objects by transform.position breaks collision resolution and leads to jitter. Always manipulate Rigidbody through its API in FixedUpdate.
Key Takeaway

Attach a Rigidbody to make an object subject to physics; do not mix direct transform updates with Rigidbody-controlled motion.

Concrete example
Create a Capsule named Player, add Rigidbody, enable Use Gravity. Press Play and observe it fall onto the ground collider and settle. This shows the Rigidbody receiving gravity and collision responses.
Try it: Toggle constraints to freeze rotation if the capsule tips over when you don't want it to.
Why it matters
Using Rigidbody correctly prevents unnatural motion, ensures accurate collision detection, and lets you rely on Unity's physics rather than manual hacks.

screens.title: Applying Forces and Velocity
screens.subtitle: AddForce, ForceMode, and directly setting velocity

narration.text: There are two common ways to control a Rigidbody: apply forces with AddForce, or directly set the velocity property. AddForce is used when you want physics-like acceleration. It lets mass, drag, and other physical properties shape the result. ForceMode controls how that force is applied; for example, ForceMode. Impulse gives an instant impulse, useful for jumps, while ForceMode. Force applies a continuous push. Directly setting Rigidbody. velocity is useful when you need precise control over speed and direction, such as a top-down movement where you want immediate response. A typical pattern for a grounded player: inside FixedUpdate read Input. GetAxis, build a movement vector, normalize it to prevent faster diagonals, multiply by moveSpeed, and set rb. velocity while preserving the Y value for gravity. A misconception is thinking AddForce always gives realistic motion; if you need precise character control it can feel floaty unless tuned. Try both approaches to feel the difference and choose the one that matches your gameplay goals. Applying Forces and Velocity means use addforce for accelerative, physics-driven motion and velocity for direct, precise speed control; choose based on desired gameplay feel.. In practical terms, addforce, forcemode, and directly setting velocity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Force vs Velocity
keyIdea.text: Use AddForce for accelerative, physics-driven motion and velocity for direct, precise speed control; choose based on desired gameplay feel.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Applying Forces and Velocity
Step-by-step: AddForce
  1. Call rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse) to jump.
  2. Use ForceMode.Force for continuous pushes like wind.
  3. Tune mass and drag to shape acceleration and damping.
Step-by-step: velocity
  1. Compute movement vector from input and orientation.
  2. Normalize to avoid diagonal speed spikes.
  3. Set rb.velocity = new Vector3(move.x, rb.velocity.y, move.z) for direct control.
Common mistake

Using AddForce for tight character control without tuning can make movement feel slippery; consider direct velocity for arcade-like responses.

Concrete example
Inside FixedUpdate compute horizontal and vertical Input.GetAxis, build movement using transform.right and transform.forward, normalize, multiply by moveSpeed, then set rb.velocity while preserving current Y for gravity and jumps.
Key takeaway
Pick AddForce for emergent physics and velocity for deterministic movement. Tune mass, drag, and ForceMode to match the game's feel.

screens.title: Collision vs Trigger
screens.subtitle: When to use OnCollisionEnter and when to use OnTriggerEnter

narration.text: Collision and trigger events both detect contact but serve different gameplay needs. Collisions occur between non-trigger colliders when at least one object has a Rigidbody. They produce OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit callbacks and represent solid physical interactions where objects cannot pass through each other. Use collisions when you need physical responses such as bouncing, blocking movement, or applying forces on contact. Triggers are colliders with Is Trigger checked. They let objects pass through while still firing OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit if at least one object has a Rigidbody. Use triggers for detection zones, pickups, or area effects where you do not want a physical stop. A common mistake is forgetting that at least one of the pair must have a Rigidbody for callbacks to occur. Also avoid making the ground a trigger if you expect the player to land on it. To test, make a collectible sphere with Is Trigger checked and implement OnTriggerEnter to Destroy the object when the player enters the area. That concrete test clarifies the difference quickly. Collision vs Trigger means collisions are for physical interactions and blocking; triggers are for detection without physical obstruction. at least one rigidbody is required for callbacks.. In practical terms, when to use oncollisionenter and when to use ontriggerenter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Collision vs Trigger
keyIdea.text: Collisions are for physical interactions and blocking; triggers are for detection without physical obstruction. At least one Rigidbody is required for callbacks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Collision vs Trigger
At-a-glance
Collision
OnCollisionEnter, solid, prevents overlap, needs colliders and Rigidbody on at least one side.
Trigger
OnTriggerEnter, non-physical detection, Is Trigger checked, used for pickups and zones.
Common pitfalls
  • Neither object has a Rigidbody — no callbacks will fire.
  • Making a ground collider a trigger prevents landing interactions.
  • Large collider sizes can cause unexpected overlaps on spawn.
Concrete example
Create a Collectible sphere with a SphereCollider and check Is Trigger. Tag it Collectible. In the player script use OnTriggerEnter to Detect and Destroy the collectible. This shows detection without blocking movement.
Key Takeaway

Use collisions for physical interactions and triggers for detection-only zones; ensure at least one Rigidbody exists between interactors.

screens.title: Collider Types and Configuration
screens.subtitle: Choosing shapes and settings for reliable detection

narration.text: Colliders define the physical shape used for collision detection. Common 3D types are BoxCollider, SphereCollider, and CapsuleCollider. Each has trade-offs: boxes give simple axis-aligned bounds, spheres are cheap for radial checks, and capsules are useful for upright characters because they slide smoothly over geometry. Configure collider size and center carefully so it matches the visual mesh. If the collider is too small or offset, collisions may appear to miss. The Is Trigger checkbox switches the collider from a solid into a sensor that fires trigger events. Remember that colliders alone do not trigger physics callbacks unless at least one object has a Rigidbody. For characters, keep a non-trigger collider for solid ground interactions and add a separate trigger child collider for detection zones like attack ranges or pickup radii. A practical tip: use a child object with a smaller trigger collider to handle pickups so you retain robust physical response on the main collider. This pattern prevents accidental passthroughs while providing clean detection zones. Collider Types and Configuration means match collider shapes to object geometry, use child triggers for detection, and keep at least one rigidbody present for events.. In practical terms, choosing shapes and settings for reliable detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SphereCollider
Cheap radial checks, useful for projectiles or simple pickups.
CapsuleCollider

Configuration tips

  • Use child trigger colliders for pickup ranges or close-proximity sensors.
  • Check that ground colliders are not triggers if you expect landing and solid contact.
Pro tip

If your player falls through the ground, ensure both player and ground have colliders, and the ground is not set as a trigger.

screens.title: PlayerMovement Script Explained
screens.subtitle: Line-by-line guided reading of a Rigidbody-based movement script

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical player controller pattern that uses Rigidbody for movement and the legacy Input Manager for controls. The script requires a Rigidbody component and caches it in Awake for efficiency. Inside FixedUpdate it reads Input. GetAxis for horizontal and vertical values, builds a movement vector using the object's transform directions, normalizes it to avoid diagonal speed boosts, and multiplies by moveSpeed to obtain a target horizontal velocity. It then assigns rb. velocity while preserving the Y component so gravity and jumps remain independent. For jumping, it checks Input. GetButtonDown("Jump") and a simple isGrounded boolean to avoid double jumps, then calls rb. AddForce(Vector3. up * jumpForce, ForceMode. Impulse) to apply an instant upward impulse. OnCollisionEnter flips isGrounded back to true when the player contacts ground tagged appropriately. OnTriggerEnter handles pickups by checking tags and destroying the collectible. A common misconception is performing Input reads and physics in Update and FixedUpdate inconsistently; keep physics in FixedUpdate and input polling can be captured in Update and transferred if needed. PlayerMovement Script Explained means cache rigidbody in awake, read input, compute movement in fixedupdate, set velocity preserving vertical velocity, and use addforce with forcemode.impulse for jumps.. In practical terms, line-by-line guided reading of a rigidbody-based movement script. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: Cache Rigidbody in Awake, read input, compute movement in FixedUpdate, set velocity preserving vertical velocity, and use AddForce with ForceMode.Impulse for jumps.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › PlayerMovement.cs 
// PlayerMovement.cs - excerpt
using UnityEngine;

[RequireComponent(typeof(Rigidbody))]
public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5.0f;
  public float jumpForce = 8.0f;
  private Rigidbody rb;
  private bool isGrounded = true;

  void Awake()
  {
    rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
  }

  void FixedUpdate()
  {
    float moveHorizontal = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
    float moveVertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

    Vector3 movement = transform.right * moveHorizontal + transform.forward * moveVertical;
    movement = movement.normalized * moveSpeed;

    rb.velocity = new Vector3(movement.x, rb.velocity.y, movement.z);

    if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
    {
      rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
      isGrounded = false;
    }
  }

  void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
  {
    if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Ground")) isGrounded = true;
  }
}
Explanation
  • Awake caches the Rigidbody once for performance.
  • FixedUpdate keeps physics stable; read axes and update velocity here.
  • Jump uses AddForce with ForceMode.Impulse and a grounded boolean to guard double jumps.
Check your understanding

Why preserve rb.velocity.y when setting horizontal velocity? Answer: to allow gravity and vertical forces to continue acting independently from horizontal control.

screens.title: FixedUpdate and Physics Timing
screens.subtitle: Why physics code belongs in FixedUpdate

narration.text: FixedUpdate runs at a fixed timestep and is the correct place for Rigidbody manipulations. Because Update runs at an unpredictable frame rate, performing physics operations there leads to inconsistent forces and missed collisions on slow or variable machines. For example, if you apply a constant force inside Update, the amount of force applied per second will vary with frame rate. FixedUpdate batches physics calculations at steady intervals which keeps simulation deterministic and stable. A concrete example: read input axes and compute the desired movement vector in Update if you prefer immediate input sampling, but apply forces or set rb. velocity inside FixedUpdate to ensure the physics engine sees consistent changes. A common misconception is that FixedUpdate is always synchronous with rendering; it is not. Because FixedUpdate runs independently, you might see an offset between visual frames and physics updates. To avoid this, keep interpolation settings on the Rigidbody or choose to sample input in Update and store it for use in FixedUpdate. This keeps control responsive while preserving physics stability. FixedUpdate and Physics Timing means use fixedupdate for physics operations; sample input in update if needed and apply stored values in fixedupdate to combine responsiveness with deterministic physics.. In practical terms, why physics code belongs in fixedupdate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Timing
keyIdea.text: Use FixedUpdate for physics operations; sample input in Update if needed and apply stored values in FixedUpdate to combine responsiveness with deterministic physics.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › FixedUpdate and Physics Timing
Why FixedUpdate
FixedUpdate runs at a steady rate. Physics engines expect stable timesteps so collisions and integrators behave consistently across machines.
Recommended pattern
  1. Read instantaneous input in Update and store it.
  2. Use the stored input in FixedUpdate to apply forces or set velocity.
  3. Enable Rigidbody interpolation to smooth visuals between physics steps if needed.
Concrete example
In Update: float h = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal"); store h. In FixedUpdate: apply stored h to transform movement via rb.velocity or AddForce. This ensures physics runs with stable inputs each fixed step.
Misconception

Do not assume physics and rendering are locked; they run on different schedules. Use interpolation or store input to coordinate them.

screens.title: Grounded Checks and Jumping
screens.subtitle: Reliable detection for single jumps and preventing double jumps

narration.text: A reliable grounded check prevents infinite jumping and ensures predictable jump behavior. The simple approach in the example script uses a boolean isGrounded set to true when OnCollisionEnter detects collision with an object tagged Ground, and set to false when the jump is performed. This works for many designs but can fail on uneven terrain or when colliders briefly separate. Alternatives include raycasting downwards to test for ground within a small distance, or using a small overlap-sphere under the player with a layer mask to detect ground surfaces. A concrete example: when the player presses the Jump button and isGrounded is true, call rb. AddForce with ForceMode. Impulse and immediately set isGrounded to false to avoid repeated impulses from a single input. A common mistake is relying solely on collision events without confirming contact normal or using tags carefully; you might treat a wall as ground. Consider checking the collision normal or using layers so only intended ground surfaces set the grounded flag. This makes jumping robust and less likely to trigger mid-air. Grounded Checks and Jumping means use collision detection, raycasts, or overlap tests to confirm ground contact; avoid setting grounded from touching vertical surfaces by checking contact normals or layers.. In practical terms, reliable detection for single jumps and preventing double jumps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ground check
keyIdea.text: Use collision detection, raycasts, or overlap tests to confirm ground contact; avoid setting grounded from touching vertical surfaces by checking contact normals or layers.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Grounded Checks
Simple collision-based check
Set isGrounded true in OnCollisionEnter when you detect the Ground tag. Use this for straightforward platforms and flat surfaces.
Robust alternatives
  • Raycast down to check distance to ground and confirm contact normal.
  • Use Physics.OverlapSphere with a layer mask for ground detection.
  • Check contact normals in Collision.contacts to avoid walls setting grounded true.
Concrete example
OnCollisionEnter checks collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Ground"); set isGrounded = true. On jump, call AddForce with ForceMode.Impulse and set isGrounded = false to avoid double-apply.
Common mistake

Treating any collision as ground can allow wall-jumping. Filter by tag, layer, or contact normal to ensure correct behavior.

screens.title: Scene Setup: Player, Ground, Collectibles
screens.subtitle: A stepwise lab checklist you can follow in the Editor

narration.text: Follow these hands-on steps to build the test scene and validate physics and input behaviors. First, add a Plane and tag it Ground. Ensure the Plane has a collider and Is Trigger is unchecked so it provides a solid surface. Second, create a Capsule named Player, add a Rigidbody, and confirm Use Gravity is checked. The Capsule should also have a CapsuleCollider. Third, create a Sphere, name it Collectible, add a SphereCollider, check Is Trigger, and tag it Collectible. Make it a prefab and place a few in the scene. Fourth, attach the PlayerMovement script to the Player and set moveSpeed and jumpForce in the Inspector. Run the scene, move with WASD or arrow keys, and press Space to jump. When the Player collides with the Ground the isGrounded flag should become true; entering a Collectible trigger should log a collection and remove the sphere. If things fail, check Rigidbody presence, Collider mode, and that FixedUpdate is used for physics code. These steps give you a reproducible test bed to learn from. screens.title: Troubleshooting Collisions and Triggers
screens.subtitle: Checklist for why collisions or triggers may not fire

narration.text: When collision or trigger callbacks don't fire, a small checklist usually finds the issue quickly. First, check that at least one of the two interacting GameObjects has a Rigidbody; without it Unity will not generate collision or trigger events. Second, verify whether the collider intended to be a trigger has Is Trigger checked; conversely ensure ground or walls are not accidentally set as triggers if you expect physical blocking. Third, inspect collider sizes and positions — misaligned or too-small colliders can miss contact at high speeds or on spawn. Fourth, confirm that tags and layers used in CompareTag checks actually match the GameObjects in the scene. Fifth, ensure physics code runs in FixedUpdate when manipulating Rigidbody, and avoid direct transform changes for physics-driven objects. A concrete debugging step is to add Debug. Log statements in OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter to confirm whether callbacks run at all, then check sibling components and prefab overrides. These focused checks save time and prevent chasing complex issues that are usually configuration errors. Troubleshooting Collisions and Triggers means verify rigidbody presence, collider is trigger state, collider alignment and sizes, tag names, and that physics code runs in fixedupdate.. In practical terms, checklist for why collisions or triggers may not fire. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Troubleshooting
Quick checklist
  • Is at least one object using a Rigidbody?
  • Is the collider marked Is Trigger correctly?
  • Are tag names and layer masks correct?
  • Are colliders aligned and sized to match the visual mesh?
Debug step
Add Debug.Log to OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter to see if callbacks fire. Use logs to narrow down whether the issue is physics, tags, or collider alignment.
Common error

Mixing transform.position updates with Rigidbody motion can cause missed collisions and jitter. Use Rigidbody APIs for physics objects.

Concrete fix
If player doesn't collect pickups, verify Collectible has Is Trigger checked and Player has Rigidbody. If not, set them accordingly and re-run the test.

screens.title: Assessment: Damage Zones and Immediate Velocity Changes
screens.subtitle: Apply triggers for damage and use velocity/Impulse for springs

narration.text: This assessment asks you to configure two gameplay responses. First, create a Lava or DeathZone that deals damage but does not physically block the player. Set a collider on the lava object and check Is Trigger. Use OnTriggerEnter in the player's script to detect the lava tag and apply damage or respawn logic. This demonstrates use of trigger events for non-physical effects. Second, implement a spring surface that immediately stops horizontal motion and launches the player upward. To stop horizontal movement set rb. velocity = new Vector3(0, rb. velocity. y, 0) so X and Z components become zero while preserving Y. Then apply rb. AddForce(Vector3. up * springBoost, ForceMode. Impulse) to give an instant upward boost. A common misconception is to try to stop velocity by setting mass or drag; instead adjust velocity directly for immediate stops and use ForceMode. Impulse for sudden boosts. This assessment tests your practical understanding of triggers, velocity control, and ForceMode selection. Assessment check

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: We will close with three compact concepts to carry forward. First, Rigidbody is the gateway to Unity physics. Attach the right Rigidbody type for 2D or 3D, and manipulate motion through Rigidbody APIs rather than transform changes. Second, colliders define physical shapes and can be toggled as triggers; use OnCollision callbacks for physical impacts and OnTrigger callbacks for sensing without obstruction. Always ensure at least one interacting object has a Rigidbody. Third, for player movement read Input. GetAxis for smoothed control and apply movement inside FixedUpdate. Use AddForce with the appropriate ForceMode for impulses like jumps, or set velocity directly for precise control. Keep a grounded check strategy to manage jumps robustly. These concise ideas help you design predictable and testable physics interactions in your game. Key Concepts means rigidbody for physics control; colliders for shape and triggers; fixedupdate plus input.getaxis for stable player control.. In practical terms, what to remember from this chapter. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts
Rigidbody
Gives objects physical behavior; use Rigidbody2D for 2D projects and Rigidbody for 3D.
Collider & Is Trigger
Colliders define shapes. Is Trigger turns a collider into a sensor for detection without physical blocking.
Input & FixedUpdate
Use Input.GetAxis for smoothed movement values and apply them in FixedUpdate to modify Rigidbody for stable physics.
Summary Takeaway

Combine Rigidbody, correct colliders, and FixedUpdate-driven input handling to create predictable, testable gameplay movement and interactions.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three final reminders to apply in your scenes

narration.text: Keep three reminders when you design physics interactions. One, always pick the correct Rigidbody type for your project and manipulate physics through Rigidbody APIs, not transform changes. Two, choose colliders and trigger settings based on whether you want physical blocking or event detection, and ensure at least one Rigidbody exists between interactors. Three, keep input responsive and physics stable by sampling controls and applying movement in FixedUpdate, using AddForce with ForceMode. Impulse for jumps and direct velocity changes when you need exact speed control. These rules will make debugging easier and your gameplay feel more polished. Before concluding, ask yourself: does this interaction require a physical block or just a detection? That question will guide your choice of collider mode and event handler. Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Final Reminders
Use Rigidbody APIs
Avoid direct transform changes on physics objects.
Colliders & Triggers
Choose solid colliders for physics, triggers for detection-only zones.
FixedUpdate & Input
Sample input and apply it in FixedUpdate to keep physics steady and controls responsive.
Closing Thought

When in doubt, ask whether the interaction needs a physical block or just a detection. That choice shapes colliders, Rigidbody use, and callback selection.
